section.title: Laws of Worship and Servants
section.sectionRationale: Immediately after the Ten Commandments, God gives Israel case law, the Book of the Covenant begins here, showing how the ten words play out in the details of ordinary life: how to worship rightly, how to treat those in servitude, and how to handle violence, injury, and loss between neighbors.
section.thesis: The LORD instructs Israel to worship Him at a simple, unadorned altar rather than through carved images or human craftsmanship, then gives specific case law protecting the dignity of servants, the sanctity of life, and fair restitution for injury, embedding covenant ethics into the details of everyday disputes.
section.frameNote: Five movements: instructions for a humble altar of earth or unhewn stone; laws regulating Hebrew servitude and release; capital laws protecting life against violence; laws of personal injury and its remedies; and the laws concerning an ox that gores, closing the section.

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses, “This is what you are to tell the Israelites: ‘You have seen for yourselves that I have spoken to you from heaven.
You are not to make any gods alongside Me; you are not to make for yourselves gods of silver or gold.

You are to make for Me an {{altar|altar}} of earth, and sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and peace offerings, your sheep and goats and cattle. In every place where I cause My name to be remembered, I will come to you and bless you.
Now if you make an altar of stones for Me, you must not build it with stones shaped by tools; for if you use a chisel on it, you will defile it.
And you must not go up to My altar on steps, lest your nakedness be exposed on it.’
“These are the ordinances that you are to set before them:
If you buy a Hebrew {{servant|servant}}, he is to serve you for six years. But in the seventh year, he shall go free without paying anything.
If he arrived alone, he is to leave alone; if he arrived with a wife, she is to leave with him.
If his master gives him a wife and she bears him sons or daughters, the woman and her children shall belong to her master, and only the man shall go free.
But if the servant declares, ‘I love my master and my wife and children; I do not want to go free,’
then his master is to bring him before the judges. And he shall take him to the door or doorpost and pierce his ear with an awl. Then he shall serve his master for life.
And if a man sells his daughter as a servant, she is not to go free as the menservants do.
If she is displeasing in the eyes of her master who had designated her for himself, he must allow her to be redeemed. He has no right to sell her to foreigners, since he has broken faith with her.
And if he chooses her for his son, he must deal with her as with a daughter.
If he takes another wife, he must not reduce the food, clothing, or marital rights of his first wife.
If, however, he does not provide her with these three things, she is free to go without monetary payment.
Whoever strikes and kills a man must surely be put to death.
If, however, he did not lie in wait, but God allowed it to happen, then I will appoint for you a place where he may flee.
But if a man schemes and acts willfully against his neighbor to kill him, you must take him away from My altar to be put to death.
Whoever strikes his father or mother must surely be put to death.
Whoever kidnaps another man must be put to death, whether he sells him or the man is found in his possession.
Anyone who curses his father or mother must surely be put to death.

units.label: Personal injury and its remedy
units.note: life for life, eye for eye

verses.text: If men are quarreling and one strikes the other with a stone or a fist, and he does not die but is confined to bed,

then the one who struck him shall go unpunished, as long as the other can get up and walk around outside with his staff. Nevertheless, he must compensate the man for his lost work and see that he is completely healed.
If a man strikes his manservant or maidservant with a rod, and the servant dies by his hand, he shall surely be punished.
However, if the servant gets up after a day or two, the owner shall not be punished, since the servant is his property.
If men who are fighting strike a pregnant woman and her child is born prematurely, but there is no further injury, he shall surely be fined as the woman's husband demands and as the court allows.
But if a serious injury results, then you must require a {{life|life for life}},
eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,
burn for burn, wound for wound, and stripe for stripe.
If a man strikes and blinds the eye of his manservant or maidservant, he must let the servant go free as compensation for the eye.
And if he knocks out the tooth of his manservant or maidservant, he must let the servant go free as compensation for the tooth.
If an ox gores a man or woman to death, the ox must surely be stoned, and its meat must not be eaten. But the owner of the ox shall not be held responsible.
But if the ox has a habit of goring, and its owner has been warned yet does not restrain it, and it kills a man or woman, then the ox must be stoned and its owner must also be put to death.
If payment is demanded of him instead, he may redeem his life by paying the full amount demanded of him.
If the ox gores a son or a daughter, it shall be done to him according to the same rule.
If the ox gores a manservant or maidservant, the owner must pay thirty shekels of silver to the master of that servant, and the ox must be stoned.
If a man opens or digs a pit and fails to cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it,
the owner of the pit shall make restitution; he must pay its owner, and the dead animal will be his.
If a man's ox injures his neighbor's ox and it dies, they must sell the live one and divide the proceeds; they also must divide the dead animal.
But if it was known that the ox had a habit of goring, yet its owner failed to restrain it, he shall pay full compensation, ox for ox, and the dead animal will be his.

altar.gloss: Altar, a place of sacrifice, from a root meaning to slaughter. God asks for one made of earth or unhewn stone, refusing the pride of human craftsmanship in the very place meant to atone for human pride and sin.

servant.gloss: A Hebrew servant or bondservant, typically someone working off debt for a fixed term rather than a chattel slave for life. The law caps the term at six years and requires release in the seventh, a limit rooted in Israel's own memory of unending Egyptian slavery.

life.gloss: Life for life, soul for soul. This formula, echoed as eye for eye and tooth for tooth, functioned in Israel's courts as a limit on punishment, proportional justice rather than an invitation to escalating private revenge.

basic.context: Right after the Ten Commandments, God gives Israel detailed case law for their courts to apply: how to worship at a simple altar, how servitude is to be limited and humane, and how judges are to handle violence, injury, and loss between neighbors.
basic.hermeneutics: These are specific civil and case laws given to ancient Israel as a nation under the old covenant, not a direct legal code for any modern nation or a New Testament ethic in itself. Their abiding value lies in the moral principles beneath them, the value of human life, the limits placed on punishment, the dignity even of servants, principles fulfilled and deepened in Christ and the new covenant.
basic.originalLanguages: God asks for a mizbeach, altar, of earth or unhewn stone, refusing ornate human craftsmanship at the very place of atonement. The eved ivri, Hebrew servant, must be released after six years, a term-limited status utterly unlike chattel slavery. And the formula nephesh tachat nephesh, life for life, sets a strict limit on punishment rather than licensing unlimited revenge.
basic.typology: The altar of unhewn stone, untouched by human tool, anticipates a salvation that comes entirely by grace, not human effort or achievement; and the limits placed on retribution here anticipate the fuller mercy Christ teaches and embodies, absorbing violence rather than repaying it in kind.
basic.christ: Jesus takes up the principle of life for life in Matthew 5:38-42 and pushes it further, not to cancel justice but to call His followers beyond strict retribution toward active mercy; and He Himself, the ultimate innocent sufferer, is struck without striking back, fulfilling the deeper righteousness this law was always pointing toward.
basic.god: God cares about the details of ordinary life, not only grand covenant themes; He legislates for servants' welfare, injury compensation, and even a farmer's ox, showing that His justice reaches into every corner of daily existence. His justice is also carefully proportionate, never permitting punishment to exceed the actual harm done.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 5:38-42 takes up eye for eye and calls disciples to a deeper righteousness beyond mere retribution. Deuteronomy 15:12-18 expands and softens these servant laws further. Leviticus 25:39-43 develops Israel's later, fuller vision of freedom from servitude in the Year of Jubilee.
basic.oneStory: God gives Israel real, practical law that limits violence, protects the vulnerable, and roots worship in humility rather than human craft. These case laws, belonging to Israel's old covenant life, point toward the fuller righteousness and mercy Christ both fulfills and calls His people to live out under the new covenant.

context.literary:
Exodus 20:22 opens a new block of divine speech that runs without a break to Exodus 23:33. Exodus 24:7 gives it a name, "the Book of the Covenant," the scroll Moses read aloud before he sprinkled the blood. The block has a frame. It opens with worship, the altar laws of 20:22-26, and it closes with worship, the feasts and the warning against other gods in 23:13-33. Civil law sits inside a sanctuary frame, so every ruling about oxen, pits and quarrels is heard as the word of the God who meets Israel at His altar.

Exodus 21:1 supplies a heading, "These are the ordinances," and from there the form changes. The Ten Commandments were flat commands addressed to "you." Most of what follows is case law: "If a man... then..." A main case is stated and sub-cases branch from it, as in 21:2-6, where the basic rule of six years is followed by the variations of arriving alone, arriving married, being given a wife, and choosing to stay. Mixed in are short sentences that sound like the Decalogue again, built on "Whoever... must surely be put to death," 21:12, 15, 16 and 17. The switch of voice is audible: the rhythm of case law is interrupted by the drumbeat of capital crimes, and then the case law resumes.

The ordering is deliberate. The first case in Israel's code concerns neither king, temple nor land but the servant, 21:2, and the law was spoken to a people just brought "out of the house of slavery," 20:2. Servants keep reappearing through the chapter, 21:20-21, 26-27 and 32, so the most vulnerable member of the household is never out of view for long. The capital laws loosely echo the second table of the Decalogue: life in 21:12-14, parents in 21:15 and 17, and stealing a person in 21:16. The chapter ends in the most ordinary corner of farm life, oxen and open pits, 21:28-36, and it runs straight on into the property laws of chapter 22.
context.historical:
Israel was not the first people in the ancient Near East to write down law. Collections survive from Mesopotamia, the best known being the laws of Hammurabi of Babylon, which are centuries older than Moses on any dating. They share a good deal with Exodus 21: debt servitude, injuries in a brawl, a blow that causes a pregnant woman to lose her child, and even the goring ox whose owner had been warned. The shared form shows that God spoke into a legal world Israel already knew.

The differences show what was new. In Hammurabi's collection penalties vary by social class, so that injuring a noble costs more than injuring a commoner or a slave. Where a builder's shoddy house collapses and kills the owner's son, the builder's own son is put to death. Exodus 21:31 rules that out: the same rule applies whether the victim is a son or a daughter, and no child dies for his father's guilt, compare Deuteronomy 24:16. Mesopotamian law could put a thief to death; in Exodus theft is answered by restitution, and death is kept for crimes against persons, including stealing a person, 21:16.

Servitude in Israel arose mostly from debt. A poor man sold his labour, or a father his daughter, to clear what the household owed. The seventh-year release capped the arrangement and kept debt from becoming a life sentence. The ear was pierced at "the door or doorpost," 21:6, the entrance of the household itself, marking the servant as a permanent member of that house, and it was done "before the judges," or "before God" as the footnote allows, so that no master could quietly force the choice.

The altar law also fitted a real setting. Outside the tabernacle, altars of heaped earth or field stones were the ordinary places of sacrifice, like the one Moses built at the foot of the mountain, Exodus 24:4. Neighbouring peoples raised high, stepped platforms and carved sanctuaries. Israel's altar was to stay low and plain.
context.canonical:
Later Scripture keeps returning to these ordinances. Deuteronomy 27:5-6 repeats the command for an altar of uncut stones, and Joshua built exactly that on Mount Ebal, citing the Book of the Law: "an altar of uncut stones on which no iron tool has been used," Joshua 8:31. Solomon's temple kept a trace of the principle, since its stones were dressed at the quarry "so that no hammer or chisel or any other iron tool was heard in the temple while it was being built," 1 Kings 6:7. The modesty rule of 20:26 is answered later by the priests' linen undergarments, Exodus 28:42-43.

The servant law is restated in Deuteronomy 15:12-18, which names the woman servant alongside the man, forbids sending a freed servant away empty-handed, and grounds the whole practice in Israel's own redemption. Leviticus 25:39-43 goes further: an impoverished Israelite is to be treated as a hired worker, "because the Israelites are My servants." Jeremiah 34:8-17 shows the law trampled. Jerusalem under siege released its Hebrew slaves and then seized them back, and the LORD quoted this ordinance to them, "Every seventh year, each of you must free his Hebrew brother," Jeremiah 34:14, before proclaiming a grim freedom "to fall by sword, by plague, and by famine."

The refuge promised in 21:13 becomes the cities of refuge of Numbers 35 and Deuteronomy 19, and the limit of 21:14 is seen in action when Joab takes hold of the horns of the altar and is struck down there, 1 Kings 2:28-34. The talion formula returns in Leviticus 24:19-20 and Deuteronomy 19:21. In the New Testament Jesus quotes it, Matthew 5:38, and cites 21:17 against those who dodge the duty to honour parents, Matthew 15:4. Paul names "slave traders," the man-stealers of 21:16, among those the law was made to restrain, 1 Timothy 1:10.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The first hearers were former slaves who had just heard God's voice from the mountain and begged not to hear it again, Exodus 20:18-19. Moses records these ordinances to show what life under that voice looks like on an ordinary day. The opening line, "You have seen for yourselves that I have spoken to you from heaven," 20:22, grounds the whole code in revelation. Other ancient collections presented themselves as the wisdom of a king; these are the words of the LORD, and the king of Israel would later be told to copy them and live under them.

Moses meant Israel to grasp three things. Worship is received, not engineered: God chooses where His name is remembered and comes to bless there, and Israel does not draw Him near with silver, gold or skilled stonework. The memory of Egypt must govern how Israel treats its own poor, which is why the first case concerns a servant and why the law keeps limiting what a master may do. Human life belongs to God, so murder, man-stealing and violent contempt for parents carry the gravest penalty, while injuries are met with measured compensation. The response Moses looked for was a community in which the strong are restrained, the weak are protected, and courts judge in the name of the God who freed them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
These ordinances were binding law for Israel's courts, so in their own setting they are prescriptive. Yet much of what they regulate is assumed rather than commended. The law takes debt servitude, polygamy and blood vengeance as existing realities and hedges them in; it does not hold them up as ideals. Jesus supplies the key in Matthew 19:8, where a Mosaic provision is explained as a concession to hard hearts, "but it was not this way from the beginning." The same logic helps with 21:4, 21:7-11 and 21:20-21.

The talion of 21:23-25 was an instruction for judges, not a licence for private revenge; the same Law forbade revenge outright, Leviticus 19:18. Jesus does not abolish the state's duty to punish justly, Romans 13:4, but He forbids His disciples to treat the formula as a personal right, Matthew 5:38-42. What carries forward is the moral substance: persons matter more than property, owners answer for foreseeable harm, trading in human beings is a capital wrong, the weak are shielded, and punishment must fit the harm. The church lives this out through the law of love, Romans 13:9-10, not by adopting Israel's civil penalties.

debates.question: How should Christians read the servant laws in 21:2-11 in light of later abolition of slavery?

views.label: A regulated, humane institution distinct from later chattel slavery
views.case: Unlike the race-based, permanent chattel slavery of more recent history, this law describes fixed-term debt service with mandatory release, protections for wives and daughters, and consequences for abuse, functioning more like indentured servitude than slavery as later practiced.

views.label: A law given for a hardened context, later corrected by fuller revelation
views.case: Jesus explains that Moses permitted some things, like divorce, 'because of the hardness of your hearts,' Matthew 19:8, and many read the servant laws similarly, as a real but limited concession to an ancient economic reality, gradually superseded by the fuller ethic of human dignity taught by the prophets and completed in Christ, in whom there is neither slave nor free, Galatians 3:28.

debates.bearing: Both views agree this text does not endorse slavery as later practiced, and that Scripture's trajectory, fulfilled in Christ, moves toward greater human dignity and freedom, not less; the debate concerns how directly this text itself anticipates that trajectory versus needing later revelation to correct a temporary concession.

debates.question: Is the lex talionis, life for life, eye for eye, meant as literal physical punishment or as a legal principle of proportionality?

views.label: A literal penalty in some cases
views.case: Some instances, especially loss of life, verse 23, likely called for literal capital punishment, consistent with verse 12's death penalty for murder.

views.label: Primarily a principle limiting compensation
views.case: Many scholars note that other ancient Near Eastern law codes, and later Jewish legal tradition, generally applied this formula through monetary compensation rather than literal mutilation, using it chiefly to cap what a wronged party could demand, preventing escalating revenge.

debates.bearing: Either way, the formula's clear purpose is limiting punishment to fit the crime, not exceeding it, a principle of proportional justice that stands behind later legal traditions and that Jesus deliberately engages with in the Sermon on the Mount.

debates.question: Does 21:22 describe a premature live birth or a miscarriage, and so who is protected by 'life for life'?

views.label: A premature birth, with mother and child both protected
views.case: The Hebrew says literally that her children 'come out,' the ordinary verb for birth, used of the twins in Genesis 25:25-26. On this reading 'no further injury' means that neither mother nor child is harmed, and the fine covers the trauma of an early delivery. If either dies, verse 23 applies: life for life. The BSB text follows this reading, which gives the unborn child the same protection as any other person.

views.label: A miscarriage, with the fine compensating for the lost child
views.case: The BSB footnote allows 'she has a miscarriage.' Many interpreters, noting that other ancient law codes fined a man who caused a miscarriage, take the fine of verse 22 as the penalty for the loss of the child and the 'serious injury' of verse 23 as harm to the mother. The Greek Septuagint took a middle line, distinguishing a child not yet formed from one fully formed. Holders of this view stress that the law still treats the loss as a real wrong requiring a judicial penalty.

debates.bearing: The wording leans toward the first view, since the verb is the normal one for birth and the word for injury is not limited to the mother. On either reading the child in the womb is not nothing in God's law; harm done to it comes before the judges.

study.originalLanguages:
The altar law of 20:25 turns on a vivid word. The BSB's "chisel" renders cherev, which most often in the Old Testament means "sword." Wielding it on the stones would "defile" the altar, from chalal, to profane or make common. The picture is pointed: the tool of human violence and human craft, lifted over the altar, turns holy ground into common ground. The stones were to be as God made them. In 20:24 God promises to come wherever He "causes" His name to be remembered, a causative form of zakar, to remember. Israel does not make God's name memorable; He does.

The heading of 21:1 calls the laws that follow mishpatim, the plural of mishpat, the ordinary word for a judicial decision. These are rulings for courts, and Exodus 24:3 will speak of "all the words and ordinances," the ten words and these judgments together. In 21:6 the servant is brought "before the judges," but the Hebrew is ha'elohim, the usual word for God, as the footnote notes. Either the judges are called elohim because they judge in God's place, or the ceremony took place in God's presence at a sanctuary. On both readings the choice to stay was made under God's eye.

Freedom has its own vocabulary. The servant goes out chofshi, "free," the same word Deuteronomy 15:12 uses, and he goes chinnam, "without paying anything," the word for what is given gratis. If he chooses to stay he serves le'olam, "for life," literally "for ever," the phrase used elsewhere of everlasting covenants, here bounded by a single lifetime. In 21:8 a master who rejects the woman he designated has "broken faith with her," from bagad, to act treacherously. Malachi 2:14 uses the same verb of husbands who break faith with the wife of their youth. The law names the master's act as betrayal, not as a transaction.

The capital laws use a doubled construction, mot yumat, "dying he shall be put to death," rendered "must surely be put to death." In 21:17 the one who "curses" his parents uses qalal, whose root sense is to be light, the opposite of kabed, to be heavy, the verb behind "Honor your father and mother," Exodus 20:12. To curse a parent is to treat as weightless those God commanded Israel to treat as weighty. In 21:16 "kidnaps" is literally "steals a man," using ganav, the verb of the eighth commandment, "You shall not steal," 20:15. Stealing goods is met with restitution; stealing a person is met with death.

The servant laws carry two striking phrases. If a servant dies under the rod, 21:20, "he shall surely be punished" is naqom yinnaqem, literally "he shall surely be avenged," the language of blood vengeance applied to a slave's death. The next verse's "since the servant is his property" is literally "for he is his silver," a blunt acknowledgment of the economic loss the master has already borne. Then the key preposition of the talion, tachat, "in place of," reappears in 21:26-27: the servant goes free "for" his eye and "for" his tooth. The same word that measures a penalty now measures a release. The Septuagint renders tachat in 21:23-24 with anti, "psychen anti psyches," and the same construction stands in "eye for eye," the form Jesus quotes in Matthew 5:38.

Finally, the "payment" of 21:30 is kofer, a ransom, and "redeem his life" is literally "give the redemption price of his soul." Exodus 30:12 uses kofer for the half-shekel "ransom for his life" at the census, and Numbers 35:31 forbids any kofer for a deliberate murderer. Here, unlike the case of murder, a ransom is allowed, because the owner's guilt lay in negligence rather than intent.

typology.type: The altar untouched by any tool, Exodus 20:25
typology.fulfillment: God refused an altar shaped by human skill, so that nothing of human achievement would stand at the place where sin was dealt with. The pattern reaches its height in Christ, the stone "cut out, but not by human hands," Daniel 2:34, and the living stone rejected by men but chosen by God, 1 Peter 2:4-5. The cross was not Israel's craftsmanship or anyone's; it was God's own provision, received by grace, Ephesians 2:8-9. The type falls short in one respect: an earthen altar needed sacrifices again and again, while Christ "offered for all time one sacrifice for sins," Hebrews 10:12, and sat down.

typology.type: The servant who loves his master and has his ear pierced, Exodus 21:5-6
typology.fulfillment: A free man freely binds himself to lifelong service out of love for his master and his family. Christ, though "existing in the form of God," took "the form of a servant," Philippians 2:6-7, and did so out of love, "so that the world may know that I love the Father," John 14:31. Isaiah's Servant says, "The Lord GOD has opened My ears, and I have not been rebellious," Isaiah 50:5, an image many have linked with the opened ear of Psalm 40:6. The link is suggestive rather than stated in the New Testament. The type falls short because the Hebrew servant stayed to keep what he had; Christ served to give Himself away.

typology.type: Thirty shekels of silver, the price of a gored servant, Exodus 21:32
typology.fulfillment: The law fixed thirty shekels as the compensation owed for a slave killed by an ox, the price of a servant's life. Zechariah, playing the shepherd of God's flock, was paid off with "thirty pieces of silver," which the LORD sarcastically called "this magnificent price at which they valued me," Zechariah 11:12-13. The chief priests set out the same sum for Jesus, Matthew 26:15, and Matthew sees the prophecy fulfilled, Matthew 27:9-10. The correspondence exposes the heart of the betrayal: the Lord of glory was valued at the price of a dead slave. The escalation is that this Servant's death was not a loss to be compensated but the ransom that pays for others.

typology.type: The ransom that redeems a forfeited life, Exodus 21:30
typology.fulfillment: The negligent owner's life was forfeit, yet the law allowed a kofer, a ransom, so that he could "redeem his life." Jesus describes His mission in the same terms: the Son of Man came "to give His life as a ransom for many," Mark 10:45, and Paul calls Him the one "who gave Himself as a ransom for all," 1 Timothy 2:6. The escalation is great. The owner paid for his own life with silver; Christ paid for the lives of others with His own. The type also falls short: Numbers 35:31 allowed no ransom for a willful murderer, and Psalm 49:7-8 says no one can pay God the ransom for a soul. Only God Himself could provide one that would suffice.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ first through its altar. God promises, "In every place where I cause My name to be remembered, I will come to you and bless you," 20:24. The meeting place is chosen by God and marked by His name, not by the splendour of what worshippers build. Jesus told the woman at Sychar that a time was coming when the Father would be worshipped neither on her mountain nor in Jerusalem but "in spirit and in truth," John 4:21-24, and He promised, "where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them," Matthew 18:20. The name that once marked a place now rests on a Person, and where He is, God comes and blesses.

It leads to Christ through its servants. A people freed from slavery are told to limit servitude and to set the Hebrew servant free "without paying anything." Jesus announced His ministry in the language of release, "to proclaim liberty to the captives," Luke 4:18, and said that "if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed," John 8:36. Paul applies the same pattern to the whole human condition: God sent His Son "born under the law, to redeem those under the law," so that "you are no longer a slave, but a son," Galatians 4:4-7. What the seventh year did for a debtor's body, the Son does for the whole person.

It leads to Christ through the language of substitution. The talion is built on tachat, "in place of," which the Greek renders with anti. Jesus quotes the formula in Matthew 5:38 and forbids His disciples to use it as a personal weapon, and then in Mark 10:45 He uses the same small word of Himself: He gives His life as a ransom anti pollon, "for many," in place of many. The law's principle of an exact equivalent is not scrapped; it is absorbed into the one exchange in which the innocent gives His life in place of the guilty. Paul says God did this "so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus," Romans 3:26. Justice is satisfied, and mercy is released.

It leads to Christ by a startling price. The thirty shekels of 21:32, the price of a slave gored to death, is the sum paid to Judas, Matthew 26:15. The Son who took the form of a servant was valued by His betrayers at the price of a dead servant.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The oxen, pits and bruises of this chapter are not coded pictures of the gospel, and the passage must first be heard as real law for a real nation. The connections above rest on the New Testament's own use of these texts and on themes the chapter itself sets out: God's chosen place of meeting, release from bondage, the price of a life, and a ransom for the forfeit.
study.god:
The chapter opens with God defining Himself by His speech. "You have seen for yourselves that I have spoken to you from heaven," 20:22, and the very next words forbid gods of silver or gold. The logic is the one Moses spells out in Deuteronomy 4:15-16: Israel saw no form, only heard a voice, so no image may represent Him. God is known by His word, and every attempt to capture Him in metal falsifies Him.

He is the God who takes the initiative in blessing. It is God who causes His name to be remembered, and it is God who says, "I will come to you and bless you," 20:24. Worship does not coax a reluctant deity into the room; it answers a God who has already chosen to come. At the same time He is holy and guards the dignity of those who approach Him, forbidding steps that would expose the worshipper, 20:26. Holiness and tenderness sit side by side at the altar.

He is the God of the weak. The first case in His law concerns a servant, and the servant keeps returning. A master who kills his slave is to be "avenged," 21:20, a knocked-out tooth wins a slave his freedom, 21:27, and a rejected woman may not be sold to foreigners, 21:8. God counts the lives that the economies of the world discount. Job grasped the theology beneath this: "Did not He who made me in the womb also make them?" Job 31:15.

He is the God who values human life because He made it in His image. The capital laws of 21:12-17 rest on Genesis 9:6: "Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man his blood will be shed; for in His own image God has made mankind." Life is not a commodity, so a man may not be stolen, and a life taken in malice may not be bought back, Numbers 35:31.

He is sovereign over accidents without being the author of guilt. In 21:13 an unintended killing is described as something "God allowed to happen," yet the law carefully separates the one who "did not lie in wait" from the one who "schemes and acts willfully," 21:14. God's providence reaches even the flying axe head of Deuteronomy 19:5, and still human intent matters decisively before Him. The passage holds both truths without collapsing either.

He is just and merciful together. The same God who demands life for life also provides a place to flee, and the same law that forfeits the negligent owner's life allows him a ransom. His justice is measured, never vindictive; His mercy is real, never careless.

For worship, this means coming to God on His terms, with nothing to offer that we have shaped, and it means that honouring Him cannot be separated from how we treat the weakest people in our households, workplaces and courts.

crossReferences.note: Moses reads "the Book of the Covenant," the laws of 20:22 to 23:33, to the people, who answer, "All that the LORD has spoken we will do." He then sprinkles the blood of the covenant on them. These ordinances are therefore covenant terms, sealed by sacrifice at an altar like the one 20:24 describes.

On Mount Ebal Joshua builds "an altar of uncut stones on which no iron tool has been used," quoting the law of 20:25 as restated in Deuteronomy 27:5-6. The humble altar was not a one-off; it became the pattern Israel followed when it first worshipped in the land.

Moses restates the release law for a new generation. He adds the woman servant, forbids sending a freed servant away empty-handed, and roots the whole practice in memory: "Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you." The ear-piercing is kept, now explicitly for the servant who loves the household.

Centuries later the LORD quotes this very ordinance to Jerusalem: "Every seventh year, each of you must free his Hebrew brother." The people released their slaves and then seized them again. God calls it profaning His name and answers with a terrible irony, proclaiming for them a freedom to fall by sword, plague and famine.

The Jubilee law presses the logic of Exodus 21 further. An impoverished Israelite is not to be forced into slave labour but treated as a hired worker, "because the Israelites are My servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt." Because Israel belongs to God, no Israelite can finally belong to another master.

The "place where he may flee" promised in 21:13 is given concrete form in six cities of refuge, where the one who killed unintentionally is protected from the avenger "until he stands trial before the assembly." The distinction between intent and accident in Exodus 21 becomes the structure of Israel's geography.

The theological root of 21:12. After the flood God declares that He will require an accounting for human blood, "for in His own image God has made mankind." The death penalty for murder in Exodus is not an arbitrary severity but an expression of how highly God values the life that bears His image.

Jesus quotes "Eye for eye and tooth for tooth," the Greek form of 21:24, and then forbids His disciples to demand it for themselves: turn the other cheek, give the cloak too, go the second mile. The formula that limited what a court could impose is not to become a private claim on those who wrong us.

Jesus cites Exodus 20:12 and 21:17 together, "Anyone who curses his father or mother must be put to death," against Pharisees who let a man dedicate to God what his parents needed. He treats this case law as God's own word, showing how seriously He took the duty the ordinance protects.

Paul lists "slave traders" among the lawless for whom the law was made, alongside killers of father or mother and murderers. The list closely follows the crimes of Exodus 21:12-17, and it shows the apostle reading the man-stealing law of 21:16 as a moral judgment on the whole trade in human beings.

The prophet's wages are weighed out as thirty pieces of silver, "this magnificent price at which they valued me." The sum is the compensation for a slave in 21:32, an insult to the shepherd, and Matthew 27:9-10 sees it fulfilled in the price paid to betray Jesus.

Jesus says He came "to give His life as a ransom for many." The idea of a ransom that redeems a forfeited life appears in 21:30, and the Greek preposition behind "for" is the one the Septuagint uses for "life for life" in 21:23. Christ is the life given in place of the lives that were forfeit.

Paul sends the runaway Onesimus back "no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother." Exodus 21 hedged servitude with limits; the gospel plants a brotherhood inside the household that no legal category can contain, and that in time would dissolve the institution from within.

study.oneStory:
In the beginning God made humankind in His image, male and female, Genesis 1:27, to rule the earth under Him. After the fall that rule turned into domination: Cain killed his brother, Lamech boasted of vengeance, and by Exodus 1 a whole nation was crushed under forced labour, their lives made "bitter with hard labor," Exodus 1:14. Exodus 21 is God's answer inside history. The God who had just freed Israel from the house of slavery now builds limits around every place where one person has power over another: master and servant, husband and wife, parent and child, the strong man in a brawl, the owner of a dangerous ox.

The passage looks back to the image of God, which is why human blood cannot be bought back and why a man may not be stolen. It looks back to Egypt, which is why the first case is a servant and why the seventh year sets him free. And it looks back to the altar, which is why the whole code begins with a meeting place where God comes to bless.

It also sets up what comes after. Israel's history will show how hard hearts resist even these limits, as Jeremiah 34 records, and the prophets will long for a day when swords become plowshares, Isaiah 2:4, and when the anointed one proclaims liberty to the captives, Isaiah 61:1. The law restrains violence, but it cannot remove the violence of the heart.

That is done in Christ. He comes as the servant who loves His Master and His household, is valued at a slave's price, and gives His life as the ransom for the forfeit. In Him slaves become sons, Galatians 4:7, and a runaway servant can come home as a brother, Philemon 1:16. His people are called to live out, now, the justice this chapter sketched, refusing revenge, shielding the weak, and treating every life as God's.

The story ends in a city where "there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain," Revelation 21:4. There will be no wounds to measure, no injuries to compensate, no servants to release, because the whole creation "will be set free from its bondage to decay," Romans 8:21. The only servitude left will be the glad service of those who, like the servant of Exodus 21:5, have chosen their Master for ever: "His servants will worship Him," Revelation 22:3.

quiz.q: What kind of altar did God ask Israel to build for sacrifice, according to verses 24 to 25?

options.text: An altar of earth, or of stones not shaped by any tool.
options.note: The text explicitly forbids using a chisel on the stones, keeping the altar humble and unadorned.

options.text: An elaborate altar carved with gold and silver.
options.note: The text explicitly forbids gods of silver or gold and calls for simple, unworked materials instead.

options.text: No altar was permitted at all.
options.note: An altar is explicitly commanded; its material and form are what is restricted.

options.text: An altar built only inside a temple building.
options.note: This law predates the temple; it envisions an altar in whatever place God causes His name to be remembered.

quiz.q: How long was a Hebrew servant to serve before being released, according to 21:2?

options.text: Six years, going free in the seventh without payment.
options.note: This fixed term and guaranteed release distinguishes it clearly from permanent chattel slavery.

options.text: For life, with no possibility of release.
options.note: The text specifically provides for release after six years, unless the servant freely chooses to stay.

options.text: Only one year.
options.note: The text specifies six years as the term before release.

options.text: No term is specified.
options.note: Verse 2 gives the specific term of six years.

quiz.q: What was the purpose of the formula 'life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth' in verses 23 to 25?

options.text: To set a proportional limit on punishment, matching the penalty to the actual harm done.
options.note: This formula functioned in ancient law to cap retribution, not to license unlimited revenge.

options.text: To encourage escalating private revenge between families.
options.note: The formula's function was the opposite, to limit and cap retribution, not fuel escalation.

options.text: To abolish all punishment for injury.
options.note: The formula establishes proportional punishment, not the absence of any penalty.

options.text: It applied only to property disputes, never to personal injury.
options.note: The formula is given specifically in the context of serious personal injury, following the case of a pregnant woman harmed in a fight.

quiz.q: What happened to an ox that killed someone, according to verse 28, when the owner had no prior warning of its danger?

options.text: The ox was stoned and its meat could not be eaten, but the owner was not held responsible.
options.note: This distinguishes an unforeseeable accident from negligence, addressed in the following verse.

options.text: The owner was immediately put to death regardless of prior warning.
options.note: Verse 29 specifies the owner is put to death only if the ox had a known habit of goring and was left unrestrained; verse 28 concerns an owner with no such warning.

options.text: Nothing happened to the ox or the owner.
options.note: The ox was still stoned even without owner negligence; only the owner's culpability differed.

options.text: The ox was sold to a neighboring family.
options.note: The text specifies the ox was stoned, not sold.

quiz.q: How does Jesus engage the 'eye for eye' principle from this passage in Matthew 5:38-42?

options.text: He calls His disciples toward a deeper righteousness of active mercy that goes beyond mere proportional retaliation.
options.note: Jesus does not abolish justice but calls for a fuller response of grace among His followers.

options.text: He rejects the principle as having ever had any value.
options.note: Jesus builds on the principle's concern for limiting harm while calling disciples further, not dismissing it as worthless.

options.text: He commands His disciples to demand even harsher penalties.
options.note: Jesus moves in the opposite direction, toward mercy and non-retaliation, not harsher punishment.

options.text: Matthew 5 makes no reference to this Exodus passage.
options.note: Matthew 5:38 directly quotes this formula, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, from this passage.

questions: God asked for an unadorned altar, refusing human craftsmanship in the place of atonement. Where might you be tempted to add your own polish or achievement to something only grace can accomplish?

The law placed real limits on how servants could be treated and required their eventual release. Where in your own relationships or work do you need to build in similar limits, rather than assuming unlimited claim on someone else's time or labor?
The formula 'eye for eye' was meant to limit punishment, not fuel endless revenge. Where are you currently tempted toward retaliation that exceeds the actual wrong done to you?

Jesus took this very principle and called His followers toward active mercy rather than mere fairness. What would it look like this week to respond to a wrong done to you with mercy that goes beyond what strict justice would require?

This law protected even servants and slaves from abuse and demanded real accountability from owners. Who in your own life or community has the least power, and how are you specifically using whatever influence you have to protect their dignity?

translationNotes.note: Pierce his ear with an awl marked a servant's voluntary, permanent commitment to his master out of love, a visible sign at the doorpost, the household's threshold, of a freely chosen bond rather than a hardship.

This passage is much debated regarding the unborn child's status; some read 'born prematurely' as a miscarriage with only a fine required, others as a premature but living birth, with the more severe 'life for life' clause applying if the mother herself is seriously harmed.

Thirty shekels of silver, the compensation for a gored servant, is the same figure later associated with the price paid to betray Jesus, Matthew 26:15, a striking and likely intentional echo in the Gospel account.
